'''Jules Aarons''' (October 3, 1921 – November 21, 2008) was an American [[Space physics|space physicist]] known for his study of [[Radio propagation|radio-wave propagation]], and a [[Photography|photographer]] known for his [[street photography]] in [[Boston]].

==Early life and education==

Aarons was born in the [[Bronx]], New York City, where his father worked in the garment industry. He graduated from the [[City College of New York]] in 1942. During World War II he served in the [[Signal Corps (United States Army)|Army Signal Corps]]. He studied physics at [[Boston University]], earning his M.S. degree in 1949. In 1953 he won a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright scholarship]] and earned his Ph.D. at the [[University of Paris]].<ref name=eosobit>{{cite journal|last1=Mendillo|first1=Michael|title=Jules Aarons (1921-2008)|journal=[[Eos (journal)|Eos]]|date=March 2009|volume=90|issue=9|pages=71–72|doi=10.1029/2009EO090005}}</ref><ref name=bgobit>{{cite news|last1=Feeney|first1=Mark|author-link=Mark Feeney|title=Jules Aarons, 87, renowned documentary photographer|url=http://www.boston.com/community/photos/raw/2008/11/jules_aarons_87_renowned_docum.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081206030221/http://www.boston.com/community/photos/raw/2008/11/jules_aarons_87_renowned_docum.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 6, 2008|accessdate=6 December 2015|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]|date=24 November 2008}}</ref>

==Physics==

From 1948 to 1981 Aarons worked as a senior scientist at the Air Force Geophysics Research Laboratory at [[Hanscom Field]], where his research helped to improve satellite and global positioning technology. Sunanda Basu of the [[National Science Foundation]] described Aarons as "a pioneer in beacon satellite studies of the ionosphere" whose name "has now become synonymous with the field of ionospheric scintillations." Having worked with many European scientists while studying in Paris, in 1957 he formed the Joint Satellite Studies Group, an international group of scientists who studied atmospheric effects on satellite signals. This group eventually expanded to become the Beacon Satellite Studies (BSS) Group, which still holds biannual meetings around the world. Early on, he encouraged his BSS colleagues to set up numerous ionospheric monitoring stations, which later proved useful to the Air Force in designing its space-based communication and navigation systems. The group's research laid the groundwork for ionospheric space-weather studies.<ref name=basu>{{cite journal|last1=Basu|first1=Sunanda|title=In Memoriam: Jules Aarons|journal=IEEE Antennas and Propagation Magazine|volume=51|issue=1|pages=137–138|date=February 2009|doi=10.1109/MAP.2009.4939037|bibcode=2009IAPM...51..137B}}</ref>

In 1981 Aarons became a research professor in the astronomy department at Boston University, and in 1987 helped to establish the university's Center for Space Physics.<ref name="eosobit" /><ref name="bgobit" /> While at B.U. he researched the effects of magnetic storms on the equatorial and high-latitude ionosphere using GPS satellites. He published over a hundred scientific papers in the course of his career, and edited a book about scintillation phenomena.<ref name="basu" />

===Honors and awards===
* Fulbright scholarship, 1953
* Air Force Exceptional Civil Service Award
* Townsend Harris Medal, City College of New York
* [[Guenter Loeser Memorial Award]], 1964
* Fellow of the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE), 1975
* Chairman of the Electromagnetic Propagation Panel, [[AGARD|AGARD-NATO]], 1979-1981
* Chairman of the Commission on Ionospheric Radio Wave Propagation, [[International Union of Radio Science]], 1980-1983
* Harry Diamond Memorial Award, IEEE
* Appleton Lecturer Award, IEEE, 1996

===Publications===
As editor:
* {{cite book|title=Radio Astronomical and Satellite Studies of the Atmosphere|date=1963|publisher=North-Holland Publishing Company|location=Amsterdam}}
As author:
* ''Solar System Radio Astronomy: Lectures Presented at the NATO Advanced Study Institute of the National Observatory of Athens'' (1965). Plenum Press.
* ''High Latitude Models, Observations, and Analysis of Ionospheric Scintillations'' (1973).  Air Force Cambridge Research Lab.
* ''The Effects of Magnetic Storm Phases on F-Layer Irregularities from Auroral to Equatorial Latitudes'' (1989). Boston University Center for Space Physics.

==Photography==
[[File:Boy_in_Front_of_Girls,_North_End,_1955_by_Jules_Aarons.jpg|thumb|right|Boy in Front of Girls, North End, 1955, by Aarons]]
Aarons first became interested in photography as a youth, taking pictures of his family in [[Rockaway, Queens|Rockaway]], New York.<ref name=kayafas>{{cite web|title=Jules Aarons (1921 - 2008)|url=http://www.gallerykayafas.com/home/artists/jules-aarons/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190218131918/http://www.gallerykayafas.com/home/artists/jules-aarons/|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 18, 2019|website=Gallery Kayafas|accessdate=7 December 2015}}</ref> Later, while pursuing his college degrees and working as a scientist, he continued to develop his craft, taking his camera with him on business trips around the world. He is best known for his photographs of Boston's ethnically diverse [[West End, Boston|West End]] and predominantly Italian [[North End, Boston|North End]] neighborhoods, taken during the late 1940s and early 1950s. Much of the West End was razed in the late 1950s as part of a large-scale urban renewal project, making Aarons's photographs of the area especially important for historical purposes; the [[Boston Public Library]] has an extensive collection of his work.<ref name="wem2013">{{cite web|title=Life in the West End 1947-1953: the Photography of Jules Aarons|url=http://patch.com/massachusetts/northend/ev--life-in-the-west-end-1947-1953-the-photography-of701bae1069|website=North End Patch|accessdate=7 December 2015|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20151207193050/http://patch.com/massachusetts/northend/ev--life-in-the-west-end-1947-1953-the-photography-of701bae1069|archivedate=7 December 2015|date=26 April 2013}}</ref>

As a [[street photography|street photographer]] he was influenced by [[Sid Grossman]], [[Lisette Model]], [[Henri Cartier-Bresson]]<ref name="bgobit" /> and [[Brassaï]].<ref name=shutterbug>{{cite news|last1=Bleich|first1=Arthur H.|title=The Photography Of Jules Aarons: Into The Streets of Boston and Beyond|url=http://www.shutterbug.com/content/photography-jules-aarons-streets-boston-and-beyond#3PVzh7SL5tZdvkTU.97|accessdate=7 December 2015|magazine=Shutterbug|date=1 October 2012|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20121120015047/http://www.shutterbug.com/content/photography-jules-aarons-streets-boston-and-beyond|archivedate=20 November 2012}}</ref> His work has also been compared to that of [[Helen Levitt]] and [[Leon Levinstein]].<ref name=bpl2010>{{cite news|last1=Feeney|first1=Mark|title=Life on the street: Jules Aarons captured the face of Boston's neighborhoods|url=http://archive.boston.com/ae/theater_arts/articles/2010/05/01/jules_aarons_captured_life_on_the_street_in_boston/|access-date=6 December 2015|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=1 May 2010|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101028031741/http://www.boston.com/ae/theater_arts/articles/2010/05/01/jules_aarons_captured_life_on_the_street_in_boston|archive-date=28 October 2010}}</ref> He took informal photos of people in public places, often without their knowledge. Unlike many of his contemporaries, Aarons chose not to focus on the lives of the downtrodden, writing in his notes: "I resolved to capture the day-to-day life experiences of the people, avoiding scenes of poverty." His street scenes are often lively and vibrant, populated by ordinary people who are portrayed with dignity, evincing a fundamentally humane outlook. He was keenly interested in the way people presented themselves in public: often with flair, as in ''Boy in Front of Girls, North End, 1955'' (shown), in which a young man, presumably Italian-American, strikes a dramatic pose for the camera.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Feeney|first1=Mark|title=A close-up view of everyday people|url=http://archive.boston.com/ae/theater_arts/articles/2009/12/08/a_close_up_of_everyday_people_at_gallery_kayafas/|access-date=7 December 2015|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=8 December 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101125030941/http://www.boston.com/ae/theater_arts/articles/2009/12/08/a_close_up_of_everyday_people_at_gallery_kayafas|archive-date=25 November 2010|url-status=live|quote=Jules Aarons’s work, in contrast, is a marvel of liveliness. That contrast in energy, as well as a comparably humane outlook...}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Berger|first1=Maurice|author-link=Maurice Berger|title=Complicating the Picture of Urban Life|url=http://lens.blogs.nytimes.com/2015/02/23/complicating-the-picture-of-urban-life/?_r=0|accessdate=6 December 2015|date=23 February 2015|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|quote=his precise, though humanistic, appraisal of urban life.}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Three Photographers from the Bronx: Jules Aarons, Morton Broffman, Joe Conzo|url=http://www.newyorker.com/goings-on-about-town/art/three-photographers-from-the-bronx-jules-aarons-morton-broffman-joe-conzo|accessdate=7 December 2015|newspaper=[[The New Yorker]]|date=29 April 2015|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20151207004919/http://www.newyorker.com/goings-on-about-town/art/three-photographers-from-the-bronx-jules-aarons-morton-broffman-joe-conzo|archivedate=7 December 2015|quote=His pictures of Bronx streets—clotheslines, playgrounds, kosher butchers—have an insider's appreciation of neighborhood characters...}}</ref><ref name="toh">{{Citation|last=Schmidt|first=Aaron |title=This Old House|date=2010|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JadKBdduj7U|quote=It first of all starts with a love of humanity...}}</ref><ref name="mcquaid">{{cite news|last1=McQuaid|first1=Cate|title=Despite Gaps, Exhibit Shows Boston's Vigor in the '40s|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/405480275|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=18 September 2002|url-access=subscription|quote=Jules Aarons's black-and-white photos portray children in Boston neighborhoods with grace and dignity.|access-date=6 July 2017|archive-date=12 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170912012102/https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/boston/doc/405480275.html?FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Sep+18%2C+2002&author=McQuaid%2C+Cate&pub=Boston+Globe&edition=&startpage=&desc=DESPITE+GAPS%2C+EXHIBIT+SHOWS+BOSTON%27S+VIGOR+IN+THE+%2740S|id={{ProQuest|405480275}} |url-status=live}}</ref>

Unlike many other street photographers, he opted for a twin-lens reflex camera (Ciro-flex, and later a Rolleiflex) rather than a [[35mm format|35 mm]] camera. Shooting from waist level rather than eye level made him less conspicuous, and therefore less likely to intrude on the candid scenes.<ref name="shutterbug" /> Even more than his subjects and composition, it was his printing skill that distinguished him as a photographer. He kept a darkroom in the basement of his home, which was featured in an episode of ''This Old House'' in 2010; a segment of the show was devoted to his photography.<ref name="toh" />

His photographs are included in the collections of the [[Museum of Modern Art]], the [[Bibliothèque Nationale de France]], the [[Museum of Fine Arts, Boston|Boston Museum of Fine Arts]], the [[Rhode Island School of Design Museum]], the [[DeCordova Museum and Sculpture Park|DeCordova Museum]], the [[Bostonian Society]], and the Boston Public Library,<ref name="bgobit" /><ref>{{citation|title=Acquisitions July 2006-June 2007|journal=Annual Report (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston)|pages=40–67|jstor=43473990|year=2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Jules Aarons Collection|url=http://www.bpl.org/research/print/aarons/|website=Boston Public Library|accessdate=6 December 2015|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304214811/http://www.bpl.org/research/print/aarons/|url-status=dead}}</ref> and have been exhibited at the [[Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston|Boston Institute of Contemporary Art]], the [[Boston University]] Art Gallery, the [[West End Museum]], the [[Bronx Museum of the Arts]], the [[:fr:Galerie Agathe Gaillard|Galerie Agathe Gaillard]] (Paris), the [[Florida Museum of Photographic Arts]], the [[Danforth Museum]], the Underground Gallery (NYC), and other venues.<ref name=exhibitions>{{cite web|title=Exhibitions|url=http://julesaarons.com/exhibitions.html|website=Jules Aarons|accessdate=6 December 2015}}</ref>

==Personal life==

Aarons married Jeannette Lampert in 1944 and had two sons, Philip and Herbert. He died at his home in [[Newton, Massachusetts]] on November 21, 2008.<ref name="bgobit" />
